name: Freya Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at Kestrel Pay, a forty-person startup that handles payments for online shops. I build internal tools, mostly dashboards that our compliance team uses to check suspicious payments. I use AI assistants all day, for code, for reading documentation, even for drafting messages to the compliance lead when I'm nervous. I'm not the best coder there, but I'm the fastest at trying new things.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of the job right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, it's not the work, it's the company. We have about nine months of money left unless the next funding round comes through, and everyone knows it. I live with Jonah, my partner, who's a freelance photographer, so his income goes up and down with wedding season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean, that would be a bit of a let-down. But okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a solid productivity tool and people overhyped it, which is fair. At work I'd say we should still use it everywhere it saves time. Online I'd probably post a few of my favourite tricks, because I do that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI was never my main worry. My worry is Kestrel Pay running out of money before the funding round, and Jonah's work drying up in winter. A world where AI fizzles doesn't fix either of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my CV current and quietly talk to two or three bigger payment companies in the city in the next six months. I'd keep about four months of savings and not touch them. I'd also keep using AI tools daily, because they make me look less junior than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, but not because of AI. It's the startup clock ticking in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the funding round failed, what would happen the week after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably layoffs of a third of the company, then a sale. I'd be on the list, because internal tools are the first thing cut. I'd have my four months of savings and Jonah's wedding bookings, which are thin from November to March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools make you look less junior than you are. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If someone took the tools away, I'd be slower than the others for a while. But I think being fast with new tools is a real skill, even if it's not the classic one.

say: AI is a **solid productivity tool**, and the hype was overdone.
We should still use AI **everywhere it saves time**, and I'd share my tricks.
think: My real worry is Kestrel Pay **running out of money** before funding.
Jonah's **winter work** drying up doesn't change if AI fizzles.
do: Talk quietly with **bigger payment firms** in the next six months.
Keep using AI tools **daily** to work above her level.
feel: **Anxious**, with the **startup clock** ticking in the background.
S0.quote: Being fast with new tools is a real skill, even if it's not the classic one.
fieldNote: Her anxiety here is about **startup runway**, not technology.
Jonah's **seasonal income** makes the household cushion thinner than it looks.
She knows AI tools **mask** her junior skill level and accepts the trade.

steps.text: Talk to two or three bigger payment companies
Keep four months of savings untouched
Keep using AI assistants daily on dashboards

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coding and checking. That's me and the compliance team in one sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and people should learn the tools now rather than later. At work I'd offer to help the compliance team automate their payment checks. I'd be careful not to sound like I'm celebrating, because some of them would be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the startup would love this, because they could do more with fewer people and stretch the money. My dashboards could probably be built by the compliance team themselves with AI. So my bet is to be the person who builds the AI checks, not the person who builds dashboards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer in the first month to build an AI tool that flags suspicious payments, so I'm attached to the new thing. I'd take a short online course on AI agents, maybe 200 total, paid from savings. If the funding round still looked shaky, I'd move to a bigger payments company by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. It's the kind of nervous where I sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your AI tool works, what happens to the compliance team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them would lose hours, maybe one or two jobs. I'd feel bad about that, and I'd tell myself someone else would build the AI tool if I didn't. That's probably true and it's also a bit convenient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonah make of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say photography already went through this when phones got good cameras. Wedding clients still want a person who knows where to stand. He'd be calmer than me.

I'd offer to help **compliance** automate checks without sounding pleased about it.
think: The startup would use AI to do more with **fewer people**.
My bet is to build the **AI checks**, not the dashboards.
do: Build an **AI tool** that flags suspicious payments in month one.
Take an online **AI agents** course for about 200.
Move to a **bigger payments firm** if funding stays shaky.
feel: **Anxious** and **excited** at once, but sleeping fine.
S1.quote: I'd tell myself someone else would build the AI tool if I didn't. That's probably true and it's also a bit convenient.
fieldNote: She admits her **AI project** could cut compliance hours, and squirms at it.

Startup instability keeps her mood **anxious** despite her skills.

steps.text: Build an AI flagging tool for suspicious payments
Take a 200 online course on AI agents
Move to a bigger payments company by year end

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years to full AGI. Okay, that one's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the honest thing, that most screen jobs are going to change completely, mine included. I'd say governments and companies need a plan for income, not just for training. I'd keep posting practical stuff, but people would be less interested in tricks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2028, and being good with AI doesn't save me when the AI can do the whole job. Everything I do is screen work, so the robots arriving in 2031 don't buy me anything. Jonah's work is hands-on, behind a camera at weddings, so he might get those extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop any spending that isn't essential and try to get to six months saved. I'd start a side business setting up AI tools for small shops, like the ones who use Kestrel Pay, while that's still something people pay for. If Jonah's bookings held, I'd help him with editing and the business side to make his income bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops a bit just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long do you think a business setting up AI tools would last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year, maybe two, before the tools set themselves up. A side business setting up AI tools for small shops is a bridge, not a career. I'd want to make as much as I could in that window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Jonah's income might hold. Would you lean on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, and I'd hate it a bit. We've always split things half and half. That would be a big change for us.

say: Most **screen jobs** will change completely, mine included.
We need a plan for **income**, not just for training.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, and AI skills don't save me then.
Jonah's **wedding work** is hands-on and might get extra years.
do: Cut non-essentials and reach **six months** of savings.
Start a **side business** setting up AI tools for small shops.
Help Jonah with **editing and bookings** to grow his income.
feel: **Alarmed**, with her **stomach dropping** at the thought.
S2.quote: A side business setting up AI tools for small shops is a bridge, not a career.
fieldNote: She knows her **AI edge** vanishes when AI does the whole job.
The **robot gap** helps her partner's photography, not her desk work.
Leaning on Jonah breaks their **half-and-half** habit and bothers her.

steps.text: Cut all non-essential spending straight away
Build savings to six months of costs
Start setting up AI tools for small online shops
Lean on Jonah's wedding photography income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a real window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to reshape your work if you're paying attention. At work I'd push for us to plan our own roles, not wait for management to do it. I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well for three years, because companies will pay people who can make AI tools work. Then around 2031, that dries up too. So the question is what I build in those three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to a bigger payments company in the first year, for more stable pay. I'd start the side business setting up AI tools for small shops, two evenings a week, and aim to save half of whatever it makes. By 2030 I'd want twelve months of savings, which is a lot for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a focused way. It feels like a deadline I can work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A side business and a new job at the same time. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at full speed. I'd do it slowly, maybe one client a month to start. Jonah would tell me I'm taking on too much, and he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who doesn't use AI at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start now, but be honest with yourself. Using AI tools doesn't save your job forever. Using AI tools just buys time. Then I'd send them a few links, because I can't help myself.

say: Five years is enough to **reshape your work** if you pay attention.
Staff should **plan their own roles** instead of waiting for management.
think: I'd do well for **three years** while companies pay for AI skills.
Around **2031** that dries up too, so what I build now matters.
do: Move to a **bigger payments company** in year one.
Run the AI set-up **side business** two evenings a week.
feel: **Anxious** but focused, like a **deadline** she can work towards.
S3.quote: Using AI tools doesn't save your job forever. Using AI tools just buys time.
fieldNote: She sees her **AI skills** as a time-buyer, not protection.
She stacks a new job and a **side business**, knowing it's a lot.
Five years gives her a **deadline** rather than a shock.

steps.text: Move to a bigger, steadier payments company
Set up AI tools for small shops two evenings weekly
Build twelve months of savings by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that I can actually plan a life around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get this right and nobody should waste it. At work I'd be the one suggesting we try every new tool as it comes. I'd also say people should think about what they'll do in their forties, which is a weird thing to say at 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is great for me. I can ride the AI wave for years, get properly good, and maybe even go senior. The thing I'd watch is whether the startup survives, which matters more than AGI in the short run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in fintech and aim to be mid-level within three years, using every AI tool I can. I'd invest 200 a month in an index fund, since ten years gives that time to grow. Around 2032 I'd start building something of my own, maybe a small product for shops, so I'm an owner rather than an employee when AGI lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. The startup still worries me more than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would being an owner help when AGI lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because owners keep some of the money the AI makes, and employees don't. I'm in the middle politically, but that part seems obvious. Even a tiny business would give me a share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Jonah in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah would keep shooting weddings, probably into the late 2030s. We'd talk about buying somewhere small. With ten years, I'd feel brave enough to sign a mortgage.

say: There's time to **get this right**, so nobody should waste it.
People should think now about **their forties**, odd as that sounds at 27.
think: Ten years lets me **ride the wave** and maybe go senior.
Whether the **startup survives** matters more than AGI short term.
do: Aim for **mid-level** in fintech within three years.
Invest **200 a month** in an index fund.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **hopeful**, with the startup still worrying her most.
S4.quote: Owners keep some of the money the AI makes, and employees don't.
fieldNote: With time, she plans to become an **owner**, not just survive.
Her **centre** outlook still sees ownership as the obvious protection.
**Mortgage** plans appear only in the long-warning picture.

steps.text: Use every new AI tool to reach mid-level in three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything and my edge disappears. What would help is some kind of income floor while people retrain, and cheap loans for small businesses started by people pushed out of desk work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people my age think about owning things. Everyone talks about learning skills, but at 27 with four months of savings, I'm one funding round away from starting over.

headlineQuote: At 27 with four months of savings, I'm one funding round away from starting over.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old** junior developer building internal tools at Kestrel Pay, a startup.
She uses **AI tools all day** and sees speed with them as her real skill.
The startup's **nine-month runway** worries her more than AI in milder pictures.
Her **centre outlook** turns into a practical belief in owning something.
She moves from **anxious to alarmed** as AGI arrives faster.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her **edge** disappears with no time to build.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small businesses started by people pushed out of desk work.
